match.reason: None of the bank points teaches forces as vectors with addition and components for Year 11 VCE Unit 1; the closest, banked curves, applies component resolution only within circular motion at Year 12 depth, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Forces as vectors
card: A force is a push or a pull. It has a size, measured in newtons (N), and a direction. A quantity with both is a vector.
Forces add as vectors. Forces in the same direction add, and forces in opposite directions subtract. The result is the net force.

A force at an angle can be split into two components at right angles, usually horizontal and vertical. For a force F at angle θ above the horizontal, the horizontal part is F cos θ and the vertical part is F sin θ.
Common forces are gravity (weight), which pulls down, the normal force, which pushes out at right angles from a surface, and friction, which acts along a surface against sliding.
draft.remember: A force is a vector: add it with direction in mind, or split it into components.

a.q: A 30 N force pulls a box to the right and a 10 N force pulls it to the left. What is the net force?
a.why: Forces in opposite directions subtract, so 30 N - 10 N = 20 N, in the direction of the larger force, to the right. Adding them to get 40 N ignores direction, which is the mistake the vector idea avoids.
a.clue: Opposite directions work against each other.

b.q: Priya pulls a sled with a 100 N rope force at 30° above the horizontal. What is the horizontal component of her pull?
b.why: The horizontal component is F cos θ = 100 × cos 30° ≈ 87 N. The 50 N option is the vertical component, F sin θ, which is the tempting mix-up.
b.clue: The horizontal part uses the angle measured from the horizontal.

check.summary: No problems found. Both questions have one clearly correct answer: 20 N to the right, and 100 × cos 30° ≈ 87 N. The card and explanations are accurate and match the chapter.
